credits.quote: some solutions now suggesting that a system around the middle of next week will cut off and head south of the area
credits.claim: A storm around the middle of next week may cut off and move south of the region, though this is not certain.
credits.why: On Nov 12 forecasters raised the chance that the midweek storm would cut off and pass south, and later discussions confirmed it drifted south off Oregon, bringing only light rain to the southern part of the region.

credits.quote: A Rex Block pattern sets up over the West late in the week with drier conditions forecast for western WA.
credits.claim: A blocking pattern over the West is expected to bring drier weather to western Washington late next week.
credits.why: The Nov 12 call for a blocking ridge and drier weather late next week was borne out, as the Nov 17-18 discussions described a ridge moving overhead with dry, foggy Thursday and Friday.

credits.quote: No real clear winner in the ensembles so for now will go with a broadbrush chance of rain.
credits.claim: Forecasters are unsure how the Saturday system will develop, so rain is only a general chance for now.
credits.why: Forecasters saw no clear favorite for the Saturday system, and later discussions first called it a weak weekend system with little impact, then said they were unsure where the next low would settle, while the wetter, windier weather was pushed to Tuesday.

credits.quote: Fortunately, this system looks like it will be vertically stacked upon arrival...thereby losing a lot of its punch before coming ashore.
credits.why: It explains why one Pacific storm should hit weaker than its size suggests, which is the reasoning behind the Friday forecast.

credits.quote: Short lived upper level blocking pattern setting up Wednesday night through Friday with an upper level ridge to the north and an upper level low to the south keeping Western Washington dry.
credits.why: It names the large-scale setup, high pressure to the north and a low to the south, and says directly why the area stays dry.

credits.quote: Latest ensemble guidance suggests a more active, wetter pattern through the first half of the week with multiple systems entering the area.
credits.claim: A wetter, more active weather pattern is expected to set up over the weekend and early next week.
credits.why: On Nov 16 forecasters flagged a wetter, more active pattern with multiple systems for early next week, and the later discussions described a stormy, wet, windy week with repeated Pacific fronts.

credits.quote: Astronomical tides will also peak next week, bringing increased potential for coastal flooding, which may be enhanced by this incoming low pressure system.
credits.claim: Higher tides next week could lead to coastal flooding, possibly made worse by the incoming storm.
credits.why: On Nov 18 forecasters warned that peak tides next week plus an incoming low could raise coastal flooding risk, and later discussions confirmed coastal flooding peaking Tuesday through Thursday, with major flooding possible at a few sites.

credits.quote: Will have to keep an eye on this one with some of the solutions indicating a much further east track than the low Tuesday night.
credits.claim: The Wednesday system could be stronger or track differently than most models show, so forecasters are watching it closely.
credits.why: Forecasters doubted the Wednesday night system and said some solutions showed a stronger, more easterly track, and later discussions made it the main event, with strong winds, heavy rain, wind advisories and a wet, windy Thanksgiving.

credits.quote: This will mean just glancing blows for Western Washington from the moisture bands spinning around the low. If the low ends up inside 130W much better chance for showers over the weekend.
credits.why: It names the one thing that decides the weekend forecast, where the offshore low stalls, and says how each outcome changes the weather.

credits.quote: helping carve out a rather deep mean trough position out around 140W. This is expected to send a series of more vigorous frontal systems into the region with more widespread precip, mountain snow, and windy conditions at times.
credits.why: It connects a Pacific jet stream and a deep trough to the shift from a quiet stretch to a stormier week.
